blocks.text: Two labourers each carry twenty blocks to the first floor of a building. One finishes in ten minutes, the other takes an hour. Both did exactly the same amount of work — but the first one was six times as powerful. Power is about how fast the energy is transferred, not how much.

blocks.title: Power
blocks.text: The rate of doing work, or equivalently the rate of transfer of energy. Its SI unit is the watt (W), where one watt is one joule per second. A generator rated 2.5 kVA and a 60 W bulb are both statements about power.

blocks.caption: Power is work done or energy transferred divided by the time taken

blocks.markdown:
There is a second, very useful form. Since $W = Fs$,

$$P = \frac{Fs}{t} = F v$$

So the power needed to keep a body moving at steady speed $v$ against a resisting force $F$ is simply $Fv$. This is the form to reach for whenever a question gives you a force and a constant speed.

blocks.title: Power of a crane
blocks.prompt: A crane lifts a load of mass 500 kg through a vertical height of 12 m in 20 s. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the useful power developed by the crane.

steps.text: The useful work done is the gain in gravitational potential energy of the load.
Divide by the time taken to get the power.
State the power with its unit.

blocks.markdown:
### Efficiency

No real machine delivers all the energy you put in as useful output. Some always escapes as heat through friction, as sound, or in moving the parts of the machine itself.

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} \times 100\%$$

Because power is energy per second, you may equally use

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}} \times 100\%$$

Efficiency has no unit — it is a ratio — and it can never exceed 100%. An answer above 100% always means output and input have been swapped.

blocks.title: Efficiency of an electric motor
blocks.prompt: An electric motor takes in 2000 W of electrical power and uses it to raise a load of mass 40 kg through 3.0 m in 4.0 s. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the efficiency of the motor.

steps.text: Find the useful work done on the load.
Convert this to useful output power by dividing by the time.
Substitute the output and input powers.
Evaluate. Efficiency is a ratio so it carries no unit.
Interpret: 1700 W of the input is wasted, mostly as heat in the windings and friction in the bearings.

rows: Heat in the windings, friction in bearings
Heat in the exhaust gases and cooling system
Friction at axles and the weight of the moving pulleys
blocks.caption: Real efficiencies. Notice how little of a filament lamp's input becomes light.

blocks.title: Efficiency above 100 % is impossible
blocks.text: If your answer exceeds 100 %, you have divided the input by the output. Check which quantity is the useful one — for a crane it is the potential energy gained by the load, not the total energy supplied to the motor.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: Efficiency questions usually mix energies and powers in the same problem. Convert everything to the same kind of quantity first — either both energies in joules or both powers in watts — before you divide. Mixing a joule by a watt is the most common source of a wrong answer here.

points: Power is the rate of doing work, P = W ÷ t, measured in watts where 1 W = 1 J/s.
For motion at constant speed against a resisting force, P = Fv.
Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100 %, and has no unit.
Efficiency can be calculated from energies or from powers, but never mix the two in one fraction.
No machine is 100 % efficient because friction and other losses always convert some input energy into heat and sound.
